newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, unions reach accord on Bezeq.
newsitem.headline: Israel, unions reach accord on Bezeq.

text.p: Israel's government and labour unions agreed that 80 percent of the proceeds from the next public offering of government shares in Bezeq Israel Telecom would go to the company, the Treasury said on Sunday.
A spokeswoman said the wide-ranging agreement should settle the issues that led Bezeq workers to walk off their jobs for more than 10 days last month.

Under the accord, reached between Finance Minister Yaacov Neeman and Histadrut labour federation secretary-general Amir Peretz, the government will make its best effort to complete a public offering for up to 10 percent Bezeq by the end of October.

The two sides also agreed that state-owned Bezeq, Israel's main telecommunications provider, would raise 250 million shekels ($71 million) through a bond offering and use a further 200 million shekels from internal resources for what the Treasury called "preserving workers' rights".
The spokeswoman told Reuters that the agreement did not specifically designate where the money would go.
In addition, the two sides agreed that employees would receives shares equal to 1.23 percent of Bezeq promised them after the company's initial public offering in 1991.
They will also get 3.0 percent of the proceeds from a deal Israel signed with Merrill Lynch in July under which Merrill took 12.5 percent of Bezeq equity for re-sale to clients.
The Merrill Lynch accord, under which the government could receive $250 million if all the shares are sold, prompted July's labour action.
The government-Histadrut accord, which still requires approval from Bezeq and government officials, also gives workers 40 million shekels in bonuses for the years 1995 and 1996.

The government had been planning to float Bezeq shares domestically this autumn but the proceeds were to go to the Treasury. At Bezeq's current market value, that offering would be worth about $215 million.

The issue of where the proceeds from privatisation would flow is crucial for Bezeq, saddled with substantial high-interest debt to the government taken on when the company was spun off from the Communications Ministry 12 years ago.
A Bezeq source said the proceeds would be used to pay down the debt, which carries a real interest rate of about 7.1 percent.
